1:
Ellicott concedes that no parable has been subjected to such various and discordant interpretations as this one, and Calvin warns against the method that produces them, since to inquire with exactness into every minute part of a parable is an absurd mode of philosophising; its leading object is that we deal generously with our neighbours. Henry says the same in his own key, that parables must not be forced beyond their primary intention, so that nothing here implies anyone can befriend us if we lie under our Lord’s displeasure. Bede accounts for its position: after three parables rebuking those who murmured at penitents, a fourth and fifth follow on almsgiving and frugality, the fittest order in preaching being that almsgiving come after repentance.

Who the steward is decides everything after. Ellicott argues from the word itself, used at Luke 12:42 of the apostles as dispensers of divine truth, and from Paul calling himself a steward of the mysteries of God, that the unjust steward stands primarily for the scribes and Pharisees in their teaching office, while the rich man can be none but God. Barnes fixes the audience differently: disciples takes in not the twelve only but all the professed followers then present, the publicans of the preceding chapter among them, whose besetting danger lay in money. Wesley makes them the returning prodigals who were now disciples. Gill reads the calling historically, by the prophets sent one after another, by John, by Christ and by the apostles. Robertson notes only that the parable is Luke’s alone and hard to explain, and that the key is put into our hands at verse 9.

The Latin voices press the trust rather than the allegory. Pseudo-Chrysostom names an erroneous opinion inherent in mankind, that what we possess we possess as lords, whereas we are placed in this life not as lords in our own house but as guests and strangers, led whither we would not and at a time we think not of; every man should therefore cast the pride of power from his soul and put on the humility of a steward. Ambrose puts it in a sentence, that we are not the masters but the stewards of the property of others. Tertullian jumps ahead to the two masters and identifies mammon as money, the instigator of unrighteousness and lord of the whole world, which the covetous Pharisees worshipped when they derided him.

Lightfoot and Clarke bring the same rabbinic parallel, each from Kimchi: the world is a house built, heaven its covering, the stars its candles, the fruits of the earth a table spread, the owner and builder the blessed God, and man the steward into whose hands the business of the house is committed. Lightfoot adds a legal setting from the Mishnah, where ground is let on condition the tenant pay a fixed share of the produce.

On the accusation two notes converge on the verb. Robertson says it occurs only here in the New Testament, means to slander by gossip, and implies malice even if the thing said is true — the word for the devil being the same root. Ellicott adds that the word for wasted is the one used of the prodigal, so that Pharisees who congratulated themselves on not wasting their substance in riotous living are told goods may be wasted otherwise. On the reckoning Barnes is emphatic that this is not the day of judgment but a circumstance thrown in to prepare what follows. Ellicott resists him: the close of a stewardship for a school or a Church is when its work is done and history passes sentence — and that day was coming fast on those who heard. Clarke reads it as a demand to produce the books of receipts and disbursements, or else simply to give up the business; Robertson makes the imperative mean give back, and give back at once.
3:
The steward’s two rejected options are examined more closely than the fraud that follows them. Lightfoot asks the obvious question — is there not some third thing between digging and begging? — and answers from the rabbinic distinction between artificers and labourers: a man who had dealt only with husbandmen would be skilled in no handicraft, so digging in the vineyards was the only labour open to him. Barnes leaves it open whether he could not dig for want of the trade or would not stoop to it, and turns aside to say that begging is proper for the sick and lame but not for the able-bodied, the truest kindness to such a beggar being to set him to work. Clarke closes the alternatives off: these were the only two honest ways left him, and refusing both he must either keep up his knavery or starve — woe to the man who gets his bread so.

Ellicott reads the sentence as character before allegory. The man has lost the manliness that would have fitted him for labour and kept the false shame that prefers fraud to poverty, and he shudders at the thought of sitting like Lazarus and asking alms at a rich man’s door. Then he applies it to the caste: a religious order that has forfeited its calling has lost the power to prepare the ground by the digging that answers to education and the work lying outside direct religious activity, and is ashamed to confess itself poor and blind and naked; it is ecclesiastical or it is nothing. Wesley makes the same point in one stroke — ashamed to beg, but not ashamed to cheat, which men call honour and angels call pride. Robertson supplies the grammatical nicety that the infinitive means ashamed to begin begging, where the participle would have meant ashamed while begging.

The resolve is a flash rather than a deliberation. Robertson insists on the aorist, which no English tense catches: a burst of daylight to a puzzled and darkened man, who has got it and sees into it now. Ellicott renders it I know, or even I knew, as of a man to whom a plan occurs suddenly, and observes that the abruptness leaves us briefly uncertain who the they are who will receive him. Gill gives it as a scheme already in the head and a maintenance already secured. Barnes draws the moral, that a man having begun in dishonesty does not shrink from pursuing it, and is willing to injure his master further in revenge for being put out — dishonesty leading sooner or later into difficulty, while honesty is the path filled with most peace.

Who the debtors are is answered twice over. Ellicott thinks them more probably tenants paying their rent in kind after the common custom of the East than purchasers of wheat and oil, and then turns to the interpretation, where the Lord’s Prayer supplies the answer: the debtors are those who have sinned against God and made no return for the blessings they received; and the unfaithful party works on the lower nature of men who feel that burden, keeping their consciences uneasy and trafficking in its absolutions. Barnes keeps to the framework, that the steward managed all the affairs and so received the debts, the debtors being perhaps tenants renting land. Gill allegorises them as either the Gentiles, indebted against the law and light of nature, or the Jews, debtors to do the whole law and confronted by the handwriting of the ceremonial law. Robertson notes only that the word for debtor is a late one found twice in the New Testament, and that the steward probably dealt with each of them separately.
6:
Two verses of measures produce five incompatible answers. Gill lists four estimates of the bath without deciding — four gallons and a half on one authority, six gallons and a pottle and half a pint on another, seven gallons two quarts and half a pint on a third, nine gallons and three quarts on a fourth — and adds from the rabbis that these baths were for the temple service, being mingled with the meal offerings. Barnes gives seven and a half gallons from one set of tables and about nine gallons and three quarts from his own margin. Clarke makes the bath equal to the ephah at seven gallons and a half, and the largest Hebrew measure but the homer, of which it is the tenth. Ellicott simply reports the data as uncertain and conflicting, the estimates running from one to three gallons up to the higher figure. Robertson says between eight and nine gallons, notes that the word stands here alone in the New Testament, and warns that it is not the word for the bush of the earlier chapter.

The dry measure fares no better. Barnes offers about eight bushels from one table, fourteen bushels and a pottle from his margin, and a third figure from a lexicographer, then says the amount is not material to understanding the parable. Clarke disagrees sharply. Following Bishop Cumberland he makes the cor about seventy-five gallons, and complains that a mere English reader can have no idea of the word measure when the two originals are not only different but stand as seven to seventy-five; the original terms should be put in the text and their contents in the margin, and the present marginal reading is incorrect. Ellicott lets the cor range from thirteen to ninety-seven gallons and notes that one calculation makes it nearly the English quarter.

Lightfoot alone sees what the metrology is for. It seems a great inequality, he says, that fifty should be abated in a hundred measures of oil and only twenty in a hundred of wheat — unless the wheat measure exceeded the oil measure tenfold, in which case the twenty cors remitted came to two hundred baths, and the second debtor was the better treated of the two.

On the document the notes agree on its force and differ on its number. Barnes takes it as written by the debtor and signed by the steward, which made it binding and also left it in the steward’s hands to alter, and remarks that the haste was because he expected to be removed soon — adding that all of this was wrong. Clarke gives the same account of the handwriting and countersignature, which precluded imposition on either side, and says the rewriting was ordered to prevent any appearance of forgery; he then compares a custom still current in India, where the buyer keeps a daily slip of account from the seller’s hand and pays by it. Ellicott prefers the plural of the better manuscripts, thy documents, covering the lease, the contract specifying the rent, and probably the memorandum of the annual delivery. Robertson renders it thy writings, thy contracts, thy note, and explains the haste in one clause: the arrangement was secret and speed was essential.

Ellicott alone carries the fraud into the interpretation. By tempting the debtors with an immediate gain and making them sharers in his frauds, the steward took the readiest means of securing at once their favour and their silence; and this answers to the conduct of the Pharisees exactly as they lost the moral force they had once exercised, accommodating their casuistry to the selfishness of their followers — releasing men by the Corban rule from the obligation of supporting their parents, and making perjury easy by artificial distinctions about oaths.
8:
Four notes hurry to say who did the commending. Gill denies it was Christ, as the Syriac suggests, and takes it for the steward’s master; Clarke says the ambiguous English has made men suppose our Lord approved a wicked man’s conduct, whereas the word simply means the master; Barnes calls the sentence part of the narrative, the only thing approved being the shrewdness; and Robertson notes that the master praised him although wronged a second time, preferring shrewdly to wisely. Origen reaches the same place by another road: the Greeks make wisdom a virtue, but Scripture calls the serpent the wisest of animals, where the word means not virtue but evil-minded cunning; and commended may be used in the lower sense in which sharpness of wit is admired in slight matters. Augustine allows the commendation to stand for the foresight only: we must not take the whole for our imitation, nor ever deal deceitfully in order to give alms out of the fraud.

Calvin states his rule again, that to find meaning in every minute circumstance is absurd, since no man would patiently endure a villain robbing him and giving the proceeds away; the point is only that worldly men are more industrious about this fading life than the children of God are about eternal life, a charge of highly criminal indifference. Wesley qualifies the comparison: they are wiser not absolutely, for they are one and all egregious fools, but more consistent with themselves and truer to their principles. Ellicott hears half-veiled indignation, since if this world were all there would be a wisdom worth praising when a Church adapts itself to men’s interests at truth’s expense.

Ellicott then sets his own exposition beside thirteen rivals and invites the reader to judge. In them the steward is by turns the publicans, Judas, Pilate, Paul, the true penitent, our Lord himself, and the devil. The wild diversity, he concludes, should make any commentator distrustful of what seems to him a complete exposition.

On mammon the philology is unusually full. Ellicott takes the word for Syriac in origin, attested in Punic and common in the Targums for wealth, and reports the suggestion that it named a Syrian deity worshipped as wealth personified. Lightfoot offers two renderings: hurtful mammon, since the root also means to damage and riches even well got often prove noxious to their owner; or else mammon of unrighteousness set against a mammon of righteousness, since the Jews used righteousness for almsgiving. Clarke grounds the epithet in the deceit of riches, which promise much and perform nothing — then turns fierce, calling it a horrid and blasphemous perversion to insinuate that gain unjustly acquired may be sanctified by giving it to the poor, since ill-gotten gain must be restored to its owners or their successors.

The Greek and Latin voices press the use rather than the name. Theophylact calls those the riches of unrighteousness which the Lord gave for our brethren’s necessities and we spend on ourselves; having become stewards of unrighteousness we must not remain in that cruelty. Gregory makes it a rule of timing: let men place their riches in the hands of the poor before death, that after death they may find something in their own hand. Cyril says Christ taught the rich to love the friendship of the poor, knowing the sloth of a mind that courts riches and bestows no charity. Against any reading of merit, Calvin denies we are told to seek advocates who will throw the shield of their protection round us, and calls it foolish to infer that the approbation of the dead avails us, the Lord looking not to the persons but to the work. Robertson says the same flatly: there is no thought of purchasing an entrance into heaven by money, and the idea is wholly foreign to the context.
10:
The maxim about small things is taken for a rule by most and questioned by one. Robertson calls it one of the profoundest sayings of Christ and grounds it in commerce: the man trusted in a very little is promoted to large responsibilities, and men who embezzle in large sums began with small ones. Barnes says it holds almost universally, and that a man who will defraud in little things will do so where more is at stake; Gill measures the least in quality rather than quantity. Clarke makes it a discipline rather than an observation: a man of genuine fidelity makes conscience of the smallest matters, and so acquires the habit of acting uprightly in things of the greatest concern — can one who is continually falling by little things be expected to resist great evils? Calvin will not have it pressed. These are proverbs taken from ordinary practice, and it is enough if they are generally true; many affect honesty in trifles only in order to seize a great profit at one stroke — as the historian says, fraud establishes confidence in itself in small matters, that when a fit opportunity arrives it may deceive with vast advantage.

What the least is the notes mostly agree on. Ellicott makes it what men call wealth and most take for the highest good, faithfulness in it being to acknowledge oneself steward and not possessor; he thinks the warning aimed at disciples who came from the poorer classes and supposed themselves in no danger of worshipping mammon, and probably at one of them by name. Wesley reduces it to a rule, that whether a man has more or less he is to be faithful as well as wise. Barnes names the true riches as the graces of the gospel and the influences of the Spirit, against a worldly wealth which is deceitful. Ellicott adds that the Greek word for true here is the one characteristic of the fourth Gospel, this being its only occurrence in the first three. Robertson turns it on the ministry: no sadder story than a preacher going down by the wrong use of money.

Lightfoot asks whether anyone can be faithful in the unrighteous mammon at all. He answers from Zacchaeus, who was not faithful in scraping his wealth together but eminently faithful in distributing it.

The last clause divides them. Barnes points out that the word man’s is not in the original and refers the phrase to God, whose the wealth of the world is, against the riches of heaven which once given are permanent. Wesley turns it on the wealthy: if your steward used any part of your estate otherwise than you direct he is a knave, and you have neither conscience nor honour if you use what is in truth God’s otherwise than he directs. Calvin adds that men are more cautious with what is entrusted in charge or loan, of which they must render account. Clarke gives two reasons for calling wealth another’s — that it belongs to God, and that it continually changes possessors — and quotes a Latin satirist that nature assigns no perpetual heir, and an English poet whose stolen purse was mine, is his, and has been slave to thousands. Lightfoot dissents: to apply another’s to the wealth God gives us is harsh and obscure, and the sense runs easier of other men’s riches — if you have purloined their goods and keep them back, why think others will not keep back what is yours? Robertson notes a variant, that some editors read our own for your own on the strength of two uncials and a father, the confusion being one of pronunciation, but holds the passage calls for the second person. Gill supplies the Jewish idiom under the phrase, since the rabbis spoke of the mammon of others and of keepers of mammon entrusted with another’s substance.
13:
The saying about two masters is treated as a repetition. Ellicott observes that it stands in an equally close sequence in the Sermon on the Mount, so that it belongs among the axioms our Lord reproduced as occasion called. Robertson counts the difference exactly — the word for servant here means a household servant, the only addition to the earlier form — then puts the alternatives: either one evangelist has placed the saying wrongly or Jesus spoke it twice, and there is no real reason for objecting to the repetition of a favourite saying. Clarke reduces it to a rule of the heart, which will be either wholly taken up with God or wholly engrossed with the world; Wesley says a man cannot be faithful if he trims between the two; Henry adds that the covetous who heard it were warned that what they contended for as the law was a wresting of its meaning — there being many covetous sticklers for the forms of godliness who are the bitterest enemies to its power.

The derision draws four notes to one verb. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all render it turning up the nose. Clarke refuses to render the Latin equivalent into English at all, and adds that they thought him contemptible for preferring spiritual things to the riches of the universe — and how many thousands are of that sentiment still. Ellicott says the word implies visible rather than audible scorn, the distended nostril and sneering lip of the Roman satirist, and notes that the word for covetous means lovers of money and occurs elsewhere only in Paul. Robertson adds that they had stood without comment through three parables aimed at them and broke silence only at the fourth, spoken to the disciples — no words uttered, but eyes and faces eloquent with a fine disdain. Calvin dismisses the notion that Christ was despised for a plain style: the evangelist gives the reason expressly, that they were lovers of money, convinced that the rich are happy, so that anyone who speaks of despising riches or bestowing alms is taken for a madman — for which he quotes a Latin poet.

Bede supplies the motive from the other side: they derided the preacher of mercy and frugality either because he commanded what was not profitable or because he blamed their past superfluity; and those justify themselves who despise sinners while fancying themselves in no need of almsgiving. Eusebius, whose note here belongs to the verse following, explains that the prophets knew the preaching of the kingdom but none announced it expressly, the Jews being unequal to the preaching of what is infinite, so that John first preached it openly. Ambrose’s note here runs further ahead still, to the law of marriage and the forbidding of divorce.

The severity of the answer is remarked by everyone. Gill limits the self-justifying to the sight of men, who see only the outside. Ellicott says the character is drawn more fully in the parable of the Pharisee and the publican, where justified looks back to this; and that abomination is the word used of the abomination of desolation, naming what causes loathing, a divine scorn answering their own derision. Robertson recalls that the same word served for the altar Antiochus set up, and finds withering scorn in its use against pious pretenders. Calvin draws the ministerial lesson, that it is the duty of all ministers of the Gospel to meet ungodly despisers with the dreadful judgment of God, since the venom breaks out from a concealed ulcer — as one might tell the mitred prelates of his own day that their hostility to the Gospel arises from its attack on their hidden vices. Wesley states the chain the passage makes: pride feeds covetousness, derides the Gospel and destroys the law, all about to be illustrated by a terrible example.
16:
The verb in the first verse can be turned two ways, and Lightfoot alone insists on it. The words may be varied into a plainly contrary sense, denoting either the entertainment of the gospel or its persecution: one rendering has every man breaking into the kingdom by force, another has every man committing violence upon it. He grants the first as the received sense of the parallel saying but prefers the second here, provided the discourse is read as continuous from the derision three verses back; and he defends that by the manner of the schools, since transitions in both Talmuds look inextricable at first sight and have been made coherent by their expositors. Robertson notes that the verb stands here and in the parallel and nowhere else in the New Testament, and takes it for a plea for spiritual energy that some today affect to despise. Ellicott calls the thing asserted a rush into the kingdom, and adds that it was a rush from which the Pharisees had held aloof. Clarke has the entrant imitate those who take a city by storm, and gives the urgency a date, since the Romans are about to do the same to Jerusalem. Barnes flattens the word every to many or multitudes, as when we say everybody is engaged in a piece of business. Wesley says humble upright men receive it with inexpressible earnestness. Gill explains why the hearers could not, since spiritual things were promised them under the figure of temporal ones, so that a doctrine despising worldly riches seemed to contradict their own books. Calvin sets the ministries side by side: God is no longer seen at a distance under dark shadows but appears openly and at hand, so that those who reject the doctrine now are less excusable than those who despised it before.

The next verse embarrasses the commentators, and three of them say so. Ellicott admits the first impression is of a want of sequence and that links of the chain may have been dropped, but recovers a connection from his reading of the parable: the scribes had tampered with laws fixed as the everlasting hills, and are told their casuistry cannot set them aside in a single instance — such as the one that follows. Clarke goes further and says these verses appear to belong to the Sermon on the Mount and stand in a much better connection there than here, unless the same discourse was delivered at different times and places, which he thinks very probable. Barnes says the same more mildly: the verses occur in the other Gospel in a different order and were not improbably spoken on different occasions, the design here being to reprove men who pretended to righteousness while departing from the law. Gill offers the plainest link, that the saying is added lest the law should be thought abrogated by what was said of John.

On the divorce saying itself the notes are brief and one is remarkable. Gill charges the Jews with putting away their wives upon every trifling occasion and for every little disgust, so depraving the law they professed. Robertson gives the whole matter in a sentence: adultery remains adultery, divorce or no divorce, remarriage or no marriage. Tertullian raises the objection an opponent would press — that here is a difference between Moses and Christ, since Moses permitted a bill of divorcement — and concedes it before answering that the permission was for hardness of heart and from the beginning it was not so. Ellicott closes the circle he has drawn all through the chapter: a topic apparently so irrelevant is explained only by the parable, since the divorce teaching of the Pharisees, lowering the sacredness of the home and ministering to the laxity of morals, was precisely what was meant by the steward bidding the debtors write fifty for a hundred.
19:
Whether this is a parable or a history splits the catena. Gill denies it is a history, citing an ancient copy that prefaces it as another parable, and notes that the Papists still point out the spot in Jerusalem where the rich man’s house stood. Lightfoot is savage about the same guides, who can rake out of the rubbish the site of a house that never had any being except in a parable; and he takes the design to be the destruction of the unbelieving Jews, who would not believe though one rose from the dead. Barnes agrees there is no evidence for a real case. Clarke declines to choose: if a parable it is what may be, if a history it is what has been, and it is equally instructive either way — adding that some manuscripts supply the rich man’s name. Calvin comes down the other way, the beggar being named, and calls it an actual fact. Wesley guesses at the man: very probably a Pharisee, and a very honest as well as honourable gentleman.

Robertson traces the purple to the shellfish it was dyed from and the linen to Egyptian flax, used for mummies and so fine it was called woven air. Bede gives the dye more bluntly, from sea shells scraped with a knife. Gregory turns the detail into an argument: if fine robes were no fault, the word of God would not have expressed it so carefully, since none wishes to be clothed in them where he cannot be seen. Chrysostom opens with the tense, that it says there was such a man and not that there is, because he had passed away as a fleeting shadow, and keeps the contrast physical: ashes and dust and earth covered with purple and silk.

The name draws the most ingenuity. Gregory notes that among the heathen the names of poor men are likelier to be remembered, and that here the poor man is named and the rich is not, because God approves the humble. Barnes notes that the word rendered beggar means only poor. Ellicott offers three compatible answers: an actual beggar of that name may have been known to both audiences; the meaning, God is the helper, may symbolise one who had no other help; or, likeliest, it was a warning to another Lazarus, of Bethany, who was certainly rich. Lightfoot reaches elsewhere: since the discourse concerns Abraham and Lazarus, who would not think of Eliezer of Damascus, a Gentile once heir in prospect, shut out by Isaac’s birth and here restored to Abraham’s bosom — a possible hint of the calling of the Gentiles.

The dogs divide them again. Ellicott asks whether the licking intensifies the beggar’s suffering or contrasts the sympathy of the brute with the apathy of the man, and settles for the first, since Eastern feeling saw in the dog an unclean scavenger. Robertson leaves both readings open. Calvin takes the second and makes it the crowning proof of cruelty, that the man did not learn pity even from the dogs, guided by God’s secret purpose to condemn him by their example. Clarke dissents from the whole charge: the beggar’s desire was likely complied with, since nothing suggests he was spurned from the gate, and the later request that Lazarus be sent with water implies the rich man thought himself under some obligation — nor does Abraham glance at any uncharitable conduct. Henry keeps the middle ground: we are not told the man got his estate by fraud, nor that he did the beggar harm, his sin being that he provided for himself only. Ambrose is harshest: the wealthy draw from the wretchedness of the poor an incitement to their own pleasure, and rob those they ought to pity. Cyril of Alexandria explains how it happens: when Satan has planted the love of money in a soul he proceeds to blind it.
22:
Pseudo-Chrysostom says one angel was not sufficient, but many came to make a joyful band, each rejoicing to touch so great a burden. Lightfoot reports the rabbinic belief that three bands of angels attend the death of the wicked. Barnes notes that the Jews held the same of the righteous, and argues that since our Saviour affirms it, it should be taken as literally as the burial. Robertson insists it was the soul that was borne, and hears the burial set against the angelic escort. Clarke finds an older reading, since his manuscript Bible and the Anglo-Saxon have the man buried in hell. Wesley attacks his own century: the man was buried with pomp enough, though not lying in state, that stupid pageantry being reserved for our enlightened age. Chrysostom observes that nobody is said to have ministered to his burial, and that he had died in soul long before he died in body.

The bosom of Abraham is settled against a literalist. Augustine warns whoever thinks it bodily not to fall into a childish mistake, since no one could suppose the bosom of one man able to hold so many souls; it is a hidden resting-place, called Abraham’s because he is the father of many nations and set first for others to imitate. Barnes derives the phrase from reclining at meals, so that it denotes intimacy. Ellicott says that of the three terms the Jews used for future blessedness this was the most popular, resting on the image of a feast at which Abraham was host.

On the other place the answers vary. Pseudo-Basil makes it a dark place in the interior of the earth, with an opening downward by which condemned souls descend. Theophylact reports a stranger opinion, that hell is the passing from the visible to the invisible, the soul becoming shapeless when it flies out of the body. Robertson points out that both Paradise and the place of torment lie in the unseen world, and that the Jews believed the two close together — a detail the picture calls for without obliging belief. Ellicott presses furthest: it is Hades and not Gehenna, the unseen world of the dead and not the final prison, an earlier stage than the judgment scene, with no mention of the Advent of the Judge; and so far as the parable goes nothing excludes the thought that the torments might in part be disciplinary as well as retributive.

How literally the scene is to be taken divides them again. Calvin says souls have neither tongues nor fingers, are not liable to thirst, and hold no such conversations, our Lord having drawn a picture of the life to come according to the measure of our capacity. Barnes agrees for the dialogue, having taken the angels literally. Chrysostom sharpens the picture: the man is said to be not in torment but in torments, wholly in them while his eyes alone were left free to see another’s joy. Gregory of Nyssa gives the principle: the judgment of God is a mirror returning a joyful image to the joyful and a sorrowful to the sorrowful. Ambrose states the gulf as finality, since after death rewards cannot be changed; Gregory adds that the just, though compassionate by nature, are so united to the righteousness of their Author that they are not moved towards the reprobate.

Ellicott takes the request two ways — the old arrogance, still treating Lazarus as one to be sent hither and thither, or pride conquered and a cry for mercy from lips that had never uttered one. Wesley is blunter: here is one precedent in Scripture of praying to departed saints, and who is it that prays, and with what success? Gill reads the scene as prophecy, taking the beggar’s death for the death of Christ and the torment for the blindness of the Pharisees and the burning of Jerusalem.
25:
The one word son divides the commentators. Ellicott finds it suggestive that the patriarch does not disown the relationship, and hears the tone of pity the father used to the elder brother in the parable before this. Calvin hears the opposite: the word is ironical, a piercing reproof to a man who had falsely boasted of his descent, as if a hot iron wounded his mind. Gill takes it as a bare fact of the flesh: good men have not always good children, and no trust is to be put in parentage. Wesley draws the opposite lesson: Abraham will not revile even a damned soul; shall living men revile one another? Barnes makes the reminder the cruelty of the verse, since a chief torment of hell will be the remembrance of what was enjoyed, with nothing else to do for ever but remember what might have been. Robertson presses the verb, which means to receive back in full what was promised. Calvin adds the guard, on Augustine’s authority, that destruction does not await everyone who prospered, since the poor man was carried into the bosom of a rich Abraham, so that riches shut the gate against nobody.

On the gulf they agree, and differ about how much of the picture to keep. Lightfoot compares the pagan underworld, Elysium on one side and Tartarus on the other with a river between, and finds the Jewish schools not far off, debating whether paradise and hell lie a handbreadth apart or with a wall between. Ellicott calls the scene a picture out of Dante — then adds that no single detail can be pressed as a literal representation of the unseen world, what was wanted being the pictorial vividness that impresses itself on men. Barnes agrees: the righteous could not wish to leave glory for the world of woe. Calvin turns it into an exhortation, that since the boundaries can never be broken we should return early to the path while there is time. Robertson puts it plainly: the chasm is there on purpose, to prevent communication.

The request for the five brothers is read as character by some and as controversy by others. Barnes says the number merely preserves verisimilitude and is not to be spiritualised, and finds it remarkable that the man did not ask to go. Ellicott hears the repeated appeal to Abraham as father both as the undue trust of his class in descent rather than in God, and as a sign that the refusal was accepted submissively, with no rebellious defiance such as men have imagined. Gregory sees a man from whom all hope is taken turning to the relations he left. Chrysostom marks the inconsistency, that not even in torment does he keep to the truth, since if Abraham is his father he should not speak of another father’s house. Ambrose puts it shortest: it is too late to begin to be a master when there is no time left for learning or teaching.

Two notes turn the passage into a controversy about the dead. Robertson observes that the petition has been used to justify prayer to the saints, and answers that both parties are in the unseen world and that Abraham makes no attempt to communicate, though recognition after death is clearly assumed. Calvin is blunter, that nothing more ridiculous can be conceived than the sophistry which infers from this that the dead feel solicitude about the living. Augustine had answered it otherwise: the man’s care for the living is no proof that he knew what they were doing, just as we care about the dead while knowing nothing of what they do. Chrysostom closes with the principle: every dead man is a servant, while whatever the Scriptures say the Lord says, so that though the dead should rise and an angel descend, the Scriptures are more worthy of credit than all.
28:
The number of the brothers provokes the ingenuity one note forbids. Ellicott says we cannot answer why five, calls the allusions some have found to the five senses or the five books of Moses simply fantastic, and suggests a definite number for an indefinite one. Gill nevertheless attempts a reckoning of his own from the division of the nation into priests, Levites and Israelites, admitting that all conjectures are liable to exception. On the motive Ellicott offers two readings and prefers the gentler: a selfish fear of reproaches that would aggravate his sufferings, or an unselfish anxiety content to bear his own anguish if only they might escape, the second suiting the humility of the tone. Wesley takes the first flatly. Robertson finds the request a delusion, the man assuming his brothers will believe one come from the dead.

What the brothers already have is defined closely. Lightfoot explains that the historical books are comprehended under the Prophets in Jewish usage, and that the phrase follows the manner of synagogue reading, where even the illiterate met with books he did not own. Barnes divides them as the first five books and the rest of the Old Testament. Clarke infers that the brothers were Jewish believers who had the writings and did not let them influence their lives. Ellicott makes it a principle: the right use of lower knowledge is the condition of attaining the higher, so that more was denied the scribes because they were unfaithful in a little. Robertson extends it past the Jews, the heathen having the evidence of nature. Calvin states the rule most sharply, that we have an undoubted rule of life and no right to expect the dead to rise and instruct us; and he treats the exchange as a personification expressing the feelings of the living rather than the anxiety of the dead, since one would have angels descend, another the dead leave their graves — and if God complied it would be of no advantage, his word already containing what is necessary.

The refusal draws the boldest writing in the chapter. Clarke stages it as a scene, bidding the reader make way for a damned soul called up out of the fire, then answering that such a sight would fail our nature, so that Christ keeps him behind a curtain and holds the conversation in our hearing. He reduces the answer to two propositions: that the sacred writings carry such proof of their origin that the rising of all the dead could add nothing, and that a man must receive those testimonies and walk by them — a spirit’s appearance could only terrify for a moment and leave ten thousand doubts. Robertson names what was lacking: not wealth, not alms, not influence, but repentance, which the man had supposed was for others. Ellicott recalls a ruler who hoped to see a miracle and had said John was risen from the dead, and whom that belief brought no nearer repentance.

On the last verse three notes reach past the parable. Lightfoot says Christ points at the infidelity of the Jews after his own rising, which shows what the parable was for. Ellicott adds a nearer fulfilment: within weeks another Lazarus was sick and did rise, and that wonder produced no repentance either, the priests taking counsel to put him also to death — a coincidence he can hardly think accidental. Robertson reports the same from two commentators and adds that the verse discourages efforts at communicating with the dead. Barnes closes with a numbered summary: souls do not die with the body, the soul is conscious after death and does not sleep, the righteous are taken to happiness at once and the wicked to misery, and wealth secures nobody from the grave. Wesley ends on repentance, an entire change of heart: a thousand apparitions cannot effect it, and God alone can, applying his word.
